full_extract: W3C's archive of historical style sheet proposals records that during the history of the Web there were a number of style sheet proposals before CSS, roughly in chronological order, and that 'they contain ideas that current specifications build upon.' Nameable proposals include Robert Raisch's declarative 'Style sheet proposal', Pei Wei's Stylesheet language, Håkon Lie's Cascading HTML style sheets, Jon Bosak's HDL, Bert Bos's Stream-based Stylesheet Proposal, and C.M. Sperberg-McQueen and Robert Goldstein's 'HTML to the Max.' Several were presented at a W3C workshop on style sheets in Paris, Nov 6-7 1995.

A Brief History of CSS traces the saga to 1994 when Håkon Wium Lie worked at CERN, the cradle of the Web. The crucial missing part of a publishing platform was 'no way to style documents.' It notes the separation of document structure from layout had been a goal of HTML from its inception in 1990, and that the original cascading idea was that on the Web 'the style of a document couldn't be designed by either the author or the reader on their own, but that their wishes had to be combined, or cascaded, in some way' — not just author and reader but also the display device and browser. CSS went against those who wanted a full programming language by being deliberately 'a simple, declarative format.'

The same W3C history documents the browser battles that shaped styling: Microsoft Internet Explorer 3 was the first commercial browser to support CSS (Aug 1996); Netscape Navigator 4's support was 'a half-hearted attempt to stop Microsoft' and was implemented by translating CSS rules into JavaScript snippets; IE4 replaced its engine with 'Trident'; and Eric Meyer's CSS1 test suite and Todd Fahrner's October 1998 'acid test' became 'the ultimate challenge' for standards compliance. It also covers how Web Fonts stayed unimplemented for ten years due to font copyright and Microsoft's proprietary EOT, until the WOFF format emerged after 2008.

Tim Berners-Lee, quoted in Technology Review (July 1996) within the CSS history: 'Anyone who slaps a "this page is best viewed with Browser X" label on a Web page appears to be yearning for the bad old days, before the Web, when you had very little chance of reading a document written on another computer, another word processor, or another network.' This frames the web standards movement as arguing against per-browser styling fragmentation.

Dave Shea's CSS Zen Garden frames its purpose as remedying a past of 'browser-specific tags, incompatible DOMs, and broken CSS support': 'CSS allows complete and total control over the style of a hypertext document... The code remains the same, the only thing that has changed is the external .css file.' Participants could modify the style sheet but not the HTML, and the requirement that CSS validate made this a primary artifact of the web standards movement demonstrating how one fixed structure could produce radically different visual designs.

WIRED's history describes Flash's origin: 'Future Splash Animator, as Flash was first known, was born out of another product's failure,' created in May 1996 by Jonathan Gay and renamed Macro... it became Flash after Macromedia bought FutureWave in December 1996. Its appeal came from a blank canvas governed by 'its own timeline, split into frames', with 'tweening' algorithmically generating the movement between key frames. It 'helped animation, games and multimedia design permeate the web' and 'brought visual artists online', fulfilling a 'general yearning to create something richer than you could with a GIF or with HTML.'

WIRED's history charts Flash's rise and fall and its aesthetic consequences. Before 1996 'the web was a static, dull place'; early HTML/CSS sites 'lifted clumsily from the metaphors of magazine design: boxy and grid-like, they sported borders and sidebars.' Some Flash sites were 'absolute trash' with 'thumping bass music and teleporting ingredients.' Flash's decline, triggered by the iPhone not supporting it and Steve Jobs' April 2010 'Notes on Flash', precipitated 'the rise of a new aesthetic... moulded by the specifications of the smartphone and the growth of social media.' It notes 'an increased respect for user centered design, usability and accessibility concerns' and that Facebook's 'minimal early design stripped back the control and customisation' users had on MySpace.

Steve Jobs, quoted about Flash (in 'Notes on Flash', 2010): 'Flash was created during the PC era — for PCs and mice... But the mobile era is about low power devices, touch interfaces and open web standards — all areas where Flash falls short.' Flash's creator Jonathan Gay adds that Flash designers 'tried to immerse and thrill their audience... to emulate the TV or the movie experience. It turns out, Twitter's a better model for holding attention... People want that hit, not the immersive experience.'

Web Design Museum's Y2K exhibition states: 'At the turn of the new millennium, a new graphic style called Y2K aesthetic emerged. Y2K web design was translucent, iridescent, playful and shiny.' The exhibition provides dozens of surviving 1996-2005 screenshots — including The Planet (1996), Durex (1997), 2Advanced Studios (2000), Sony (2002), and numerous Flash-driven sites (NRG.BE, Superlooper, Future Farmers, Jamiroquai) — as direct visual evidence of the style's characteristics.

Snarkmarket (2005), written while the style was current: 'Almost everything looks like the love child of a Google application and OS X. Predominant color scheme: secondary colors on a white background. Font of choice: almost invariably a rounded sans serif, usually in lowercase. Rounded edges and gradients are the new black. Talk balloons are everywhere... Much of this stuff is Good Design, but it's so ubiquitous that it's become visual static.' The post calls the Web 2.0 design aesthetic homogenized and notes 'the Web 2.0 backlash is a reaction to the pre-fab, lifeless aesthetic it's spawned.'

Ethan Marcotte's seminal 2010 A List Apart article defines responsive web design: 'Fluid grids, flexible images, and media queries are the three technical ingredients for responsive web design, but it also requires a different way of thinking. Rather than quarantining our content into disparate, device-specific experiences, we can use media queries to progressively enhance our work within different viewing contexts.' It concludes, 'Responsive web design offers us a way forward, finally allowing us to "design for the ebb and flow of things." '

Ethan Marcotte explains the mechanism: W3C created media queries as part of the CSS3 specification; 'A media query allows us to target not only certain device classes, but to actually inspect the physical characteristics of the device rendering our work.' Media queries allow designers to 'surgically correct issues in our layout as it scales beyond its initial, ideal resolution', to adjust target areas for Fitts' Law on touch devices, and to practice 'responsive typesetting' that alters the size and leading of text. It contrasts this with the earlier approach of bespoke 'iPhone website' subdomains.

Apple's iOS 7 launch press release (June 2013) is a primary artifact of the shift away from skeuomorphism: 'iOS 7 is completely redesigned with subtle motion, an elegant color palette and distinct, functional layers that make it feel more alive. The typography has been refined for a cleaner, simpler look, and the use of translucency and motion makes even simple tasks more engaging.' Jony Ive: 'There is a profound and enduring beauty in simplicity, in clarity, in efficiency... it's about bringing order to complexity.'

Apple's Human Interface Guidelines document an evolving platform design language built around hierarchy, typography, materials, translucency and platform conventions. They advise designing with type, color and layout to 'communicate hierarchy and personality while remaining legible, meaningful, and adaptable', and they underlie the 'familiarity' and 'feedback' principles that influenced web UI: building on concepts people already know and showing the result of an action.

Google's Material Design 1 'Material properties' specification defines material through 'certain immutable characteristics and inherent behaviors': material is 'solid' (it occupies unique points in space and is impenetrable; input events cannot pass through material), has 'mutable shape' (it grows and shrinks only along its plane and never bends or folds), and can join, separate, split and heal. Depth builds hierarchy: 'Material casts shadows. Shadows result naturally from the relative elevation (z-position) between material elements.' This is the canonical statement that depth/elevation is a consequence of layering, not decoration — the physical-materials metaphor behind the Material system.

Microsoft's Acrylic material documentation states: 'Acrylic is a type of Brush that creates a translucent texture. You can apply acrylic to app surfaces to add depth and help establish a visual hierarchy.' It describes two blend types — background acrylic (reveals desktop wallpaper/windows behind) and in-app acrylic (adds depth within the app frame) — and the Fluent Design System as incorporating 'light, depth, motion, material, and scale.' It warns against layering multiple acrylic surfaces, which 'can create distracting optical illusions', and requires text on acrylic to meet contrast ratios.

Microsoft's Acrylic documentation describes how the material is composed: 'We started with translucency, blur, and noise to add visual depth and dimension to flat surfaces. We added an exclusion blend mode layer to ensure contrast and legibility of UI placed on an acrylic background. Finally, we added color tint for personalization opportunities.' It confirms Acrylic automatically adapts — appearing as a solid color in High Contrast mode, in Battery Saver mode, and on low-end hardware. This is a strong primary source for the translucent layered interfaces that precede and overlap later 'glassmorphism'.

Suárez-Carballo's peer-reviewed study 'El lenguaje visual del diseño web brutalista' (Doxa Comunicación, 2019) analyzed 50 sites from Pascal Deville's Brutalist Websites collection using Content Analysis. Its finding: 'su significado original ha evolucionado desde la neutralidad y transparencia estilística hacia un movimiento sumamente heterogéneo cuyas obras, principalmente basadas en la tensión visual, solo comparten la provocación y la libertad creativa' — the style evolved from stylistic neutrality and transparency into a highly heterogeneous movement whose works, mainly based on visual tension, share only provocation and creative freedom, attributes that bring it close to other contemporary postmodern graphic design trends such as the New Ugly.

Pascal Deville, creator of the Brutalist Websites collection (interviewed by Creative Bloq, 2018), explains web brutalism as a reaction: 'In the last couple of years I noticed a trend toward streamlined, almost neutralised interfaces that completely missed any sense of brand attributes or characteristics regarding the content or purpose they serve.' He co-opted the term from brutalism architecture because it was 'a reaction to the more frivolous architecture of the 1930s and '40s', and the collection began as a response to a growing 'anti-trend' of 'rough and back-to-basics' web design working 'outside a perfect UX world.'

Designers interviewed by Creative Bloq define web brutalism's observable features. Bruno Landowski: 'It uses big fonts, solid-colour backgrounds, geometric shapes and raw features... It doesn't care about the general public.' Jakob Kornelli points to 'bold and somewhat radical typography' and to a willingness to 'push the boundaries of its medium, especially in terms of interaction.' Pierre Butin experiments with 'system fonts, basic web colours, a simple colour scheme.' Kikko Paradela sums it up: 'Typographic. Content-driven. Straightforward.' Daan Lucas notes 'an honesty to brutalism that's perhaps missing from more polished, corporate offerings' — 'I think brutalism intends to show the core and deduct it from distraction.'

Creative Bloq interview notes brutalism is also framed as improving usability, not merely rejecting UX. Pierre Butin: 'Straightforward brutalist elements might improve the overall experience users have of an app. UX experts like Luke Wroblewsky show again and again that, for example, the word "Menu" in an interface generates more engagement than the hamburger icon (as goes the saying, "obvious always wins").' Jakob Kornelli distinguishes not playing by a set of rules from 'classic Swiss modernist graphic design rules', arguing that not following them 'has the advantage that the results tend to be more unique and therefore more captivating for the user.'

Toptal (Kayode Osinusi) traces neumorphism through its lineage: 'In late 2019, neumorphism (short for 'new skeuomorphism') arrived and appeared to offer the best of its predecessors.' It credits Apple's Macintosh (1984) and Jobs' return (1997) with steering UX toward skeuomorphism, Aqua (Mac OS X 2001), and notes flat design as 'a digital-era reboot of 1960s minimalism.' It defines three common characteristics: 'monochromatic color schemes, low contrast, and subtle shadows.' It also flags the accessibility drawback: low contrast 'can hinder readability and make it difficult for users to identify buttons, icons, forms.'

Webflow (Jeff Cardello) dates neumorphism's mainstream arrival to 2020 and its decline to within a year: 'Most track the birth of neumorphism to 2020 when designer Alexander Plyuto posted this concept design for a mobile banking app... a more nuanced and contemporary approach that moved away from the heavy-handed physicality of skeuomorphism.' It describes the look: 'Neumorphism combines the tactile styling of skeuomorphism with the flatness of modern design, resulting in soft-edged components. It leverages shadows and highlights to create a subtle, raised effect.' It notes Apple's macOS Big Sur (2020) brought it to a mass audience but triggered criticism: 'A major gripe was that there wasn't any proof that it increased usability.'

Webflow's neumorphism piece details why it fell out of favor: 'The hype around neumorphism made its faults come to light in a flash... By 2021, most designers had eschewed it for design styles that already had a proven track record.' It warns on accessibility: 'When everything blends together in a cloud of low-contrast, it can be hard to differentiate between what's on the screen... buttons blend into the background and fonts become illegible.' It also notes the same signifier problem as skeuomorphism: buttons/sliders 'need signifiers indicating their functionality, as well as if they've changed states' when only shadows differentiate them, and there's 'no clear organization or direction showing what should be interacted with first.' Future: it argues neumorphism will persist in 'limited but stylistically notable ways' for cards and subtle backgrounds 'while maintaining accessibility standards.'

Webflow's guide to the Y2K revival gives explicit observable criteria: 'Y2K website design is a style that re-creates the look and energy of late 1990s to early 2000s internet culture... Y2K sites had bold, maximalist visual choices, like high-gloss user interface (UI) elements, chunky and pixelated typography, and bubbles and blobs in bright colors... popular subcultures like hip-hop and rave culture fed into the Y2K aesthetic with metallics and neon glows.' It describes synthetic candy-bright color palettes, chrome/metallic/holographic surfaces, blended multichrome gradients, and pixelated bitmap display type.

Webflow explains Y2K material and effect language: 'One way to recreate the Y2K aesthetic is to make your website look like it's made of plastic, metal, or glass... designers were excited about transparent, colorful plastic device exteriors and 3D-looking UI. This made silver panels, chrome borders, and pearlescent buttons with intense highlights and shadows a popular web design trend.' It also notes monochrome appears in the era: 'In the early 2000s, black-and-white monochrome started showing up in tech, fashion, and music-related pages — think Apple's design system — because it felt sleek and professional.'

The Web Design Museum archive frames its purpose as preserving web design history: it exhibits 'thousands of screenshots and videos' organized into exhibitions including 'Web Design in the 90s (1991-1999)', 'Y2K Aesthetic in Web Design (1996-2005)', and 'Pixel Art in Web Design (1996-2005)', providing curated visual evidence for claims about early and milestone web styles.
